blocks.heading: Sparks of the soul in one's belongings

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach recalls that Yaakov had extracted Jewish souls from Lavan in whatever form they took: oxen, donkeys, sheep, even servants. In this week's parsha, Yaakov remained alone, as the verse says, crossing back on a dangerous night, when Esav's angel was powerful, because he had forgotten small jars.

To explain this, he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov: a person's belongings hold sparks of his own soul, and even half an apple he gives away passes on by Hashem's individual providence. That providence, the Mashgiach stresses, reaches every creature, from a leaf to a particle of dust.

blocks.heading: The birds, the donkey and the small jars

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, leaving his cave, heard a heavenly voice decide each bird's capture, and concluded that the king of Rome could not catch him without a decree. He then brings the Gemara's donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, which refused untithed oats because it held sparks of its master's soul. So too, Yaakov's jars held sparks of future Jewish souls, and he could not let them be lost.

blocks.heading: 580 animals: a bone thrown to Esav

paragraphs.text: The Torah records exactly how many animals Yaakov took for Esav, and the Ohr HaChaim counts them as 580, the value of Seir, Esav's name. The Mashgiach adds that the name of the chief of the forces of evil, without the letters of Hashem's name that sustain him, together with the name of his mate Lilis, also comes to 580.

The gift is therefore like the Yom Kippur goat: a bone thrown to the dog so that it leaves the meal alone. The Zohar read on Rosh Hashanah, he explains, links Yaakov's sending to Esav with that offering.
Since the animals were Jewish souls, the Mashgiach asks why Yaakov, who toiled twenty years to gather them, would hand any to Esav, and how he would choose which.

To answer, the Mashgiach brings the contest of Eliyahu in Melachim. The Gemara relates that the ox chosen for the Baal refused to move, until Eliyahu told it that by failing to draw fire it too would sanctify Hashem's name. Yaakov's animals, on a higher level, needed no persuasion: exactly 580 volunteered to go to Esav.

blocks.heading: Rabbi Hoshaya and the unlearned man

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of an unlearned man who asked Rabbi Hoshaya to repeat his chiddush in his name. The verse in Tehillim says the kings will return a gift to Mashiach, he explained, because Esav must give back Yaakov's gift. Rabbi Hoshaya agreed, and it entered the Midrash.

blocks.heading: Every Jew's letter in the Torah

paragraphs.text: Every Jew, the Mashgiach explains, has his own letter in the Sefer Torah, his channel of blessing. He brings the Arizal that one whose eye catches his letter at hagbah is lit up by it. Yaakov's animals, now with Esav, are managed by Esav.

blocks.heading: Who judges the tzaddik, the beinoni and the rasha

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Esav's angel is the yetzer hara, the Satan and the angel of death: he entices a person to sin, accuses him above, then carries out the sentence, which includes any form of suffering.

He then brings the Gemara that the yetzer tov judges the tzaddikim, both judge the beinonim, and the yetzer hara judges the wicked. The animals sent to Esav, he concludes, are the unlearned and the wicked who follow Esav's dictates.

blocks.heading: Why Esav had to receive something

paragraphs.text: Esav cried and complained over the brachos, and Yaakov pacified him with these animals. Had he given nothing, the Mashgiach explains, Esav's accusation would have prevailed, because Hashem keeps good and evil in balance until Mashiach, as the verse says a king establishes the land with justice.
After a digression on how the house of David came through Rus in a hidden way, he returns: this is why some Jews live under Esav's dictates.

blocks.heading: The unlearned man's letter among Esav's animals

paragraphs.text: The unlearned man also had a letter, the Mashgiach explains, but without Torah, which the Gemara calls the only antidote to the yetzer hara, he surely fell often. His letter must be among the animals sent to Esav, which is why he was unlearned.
Yet each letter is alive and gives light, so every Jew says a chiddush at least once, through which Hashem renews creation, often without grasping its depth.

blocks.heading: The returned gift is returning souls

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach asks what 580 animals could mean to Mashiach, to whom gold and gems will be brought. These animals are Jewish souls, each a world: all who strayed will return and become tzaddikim. He then asks why the man wanted his chiddush repeated; honor alone, he says, the Midrash would not record.

The Mashgiach explains that the Ba'al Shem Tov and his disciples, when someone asked for a salvation, heard his soul asking at the same time for teshuvah. So too, the man's wish was his soul's request: the Gemara teaches that repeating Torah in the speaker's name brings redemption, and he, in exile under Esav, sought it.
Rabbi Hoshaya obliged, since this chiddush holds the key to redemption. By declaring he will return, the man hastens his return; the fortunate return before Mashiach, the rest when he comes.

blocks.heading: Why Yaakov was faulted for hiding Dina

paragraphs.text: Rashi brings that Yaakov hid Dina in a box from Esav and was punished, for she might have turned Esav, whom the Gemara calls a Jew who strayed, back to his roots; she was then taken by Shechem. The Mashgiach asks why, when no tzaddik ever sought a rasha for his daughter.

blocks.heading: Leah's tears and the debt to Esav

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach answers that Leah was destined for Esav, but her weeping and tefillah freed her to marry Yaakov. Yaakov had thus taken what was Esav's and owed it back, so Dina, Leah's extension, should have been the 581st gift.
That is why the verse calls Dina the daughter of Leah when she went out: withheld, she went to Esav anyway through Shechem.

blocks.heading: Osnas, Shechem and the gift's return

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Dina's daughter, whom the brothers wished to kill, was saved by Yaakov and carried by Gavriel to Mitzrayim. She was Osnas, who married Yosef, given Shechem as the verse says and buried there. What Esav took he had to spit out, back to Yaakov.

The Ohr HaChaim, he adds, sees Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon, a descendant of Dina, hinted in Shechem's words. He symbolizes the whole gift's return; and as the Gemara in Chagigah says rain begins with a drizzle, today's drizzle of teshuvah precedes the return of every Jewish soul.
